band8Sample.text: I'd like to talk about Mr Minh, my Year Eleven physics teacher, who completely transformed the way I approach unfamiliar problems. Before I ended up in his class, I'd always viewed physics as a dry pile of formulas to be crammed the night before an exam. I was actually dreading the term when he walked in on the first morning carrying nothing except a rusty bicycle wheel and a piece of chalk. Instead of writing definitions on the board, he spun the wheel, tilted the axle, and asked us why it seemed to push back against his hand. That set the tone for the entire year. What made Mr Minh genuinely stand out was his patience with half-formed ideas. Whenever someone gave a clumsy answer, he never dismissed it or rushed to supply the textbook line; instead, he'd pause, ask a gentle follow-up question, and guide the student to spot the flaw themselves. I still vividly remember staying behind after a lab session because my circuit diagram kept failing. Rather than fixing the wires for me, he sat beside my bench with a mug of green tea and let me test three wrong hypotheses until the bulb finally flickered on. That small triumph taught me far more than any neatly solved worksheet could have. Looking back on it now, his influence goes well beyond secondary-school science. Even today, whenever I run into a knotty bug in software engineering, I hear his calm habit of slowing down and testing assumptions one by one. He gave me the confidence to treat confusion not as embarrassment, but as the starting point of real understanding, and that's why I still think of him so fondly.

band8Sample.text: One older person I genuinely admire is my great-aunt Lan, a retired pharmacist in her early seventies who lives just a few streets away from my parents. Although she stepped back from full-time work more than a decade ago, you'd never guess it from the rhythm of her days. Every morning at half past five, she meets a group of neighbours by the lake for brisk walking and tai chi, and then she spends a quiet hour tending a surprisingly lush vegetable and herb garden on her rooftop terrace. What strikes me most about Aunt Lan isn't just her physical stamina, though—it's her refusal to let curiosity fade with age. Two years ago, when her grandchildren moved to another city, she didn't wait for anyone to set things up for her; she bought a notebook, asked me to walk her through video calls and online banking once, and wrote down every single step in neat blue ink. Soon afterwards, she signed up for a community watercolour class and now paints delicate botanical postcards that she sends to family members on their birthdays. She also has a wonderfully dry sense of humour and rarely complains about minor aches or inconveniences, which makes visiting her feel uplifting rather than obligatory. Observing her has reshaped how I picture getting older. We're often led to assume that retirement automatically means shrinking horizons, yet Aunt Lan proves that staying engaged with both your neighbourhood and new skills keeps life rich and purposeful. Whenever I catch myself grumbling that I'm too tired to learn something unfamiliar, I think of her rooftop watercolours and immediately feel a bit sheepish.

cueCard.prompt: Describe someone you know who is remarkably good at solving practical problems.

band8Sample.text: The first person who springs to mind is my uncle Hung, a self-taught mechanical technician who runs a small appliance repair workshop near my hometown. Whenever something breaks in our extended family—whether it's a leaking washing machine, a jammed lock, or a temperamental scooter—Hung is invariably the person everyone rings. I saw his resourcefulness at its absolute finest two autumns ago right after a heavy tropical storm swept through our district. The power had just come back on, yet our house's rooftop water pump refused to kick in, leaving three families in the alley without running water while every hardware shop was still shuttered. Most of us were standing around staring helplessly at the metal casing and talking about buying a brand-new unit the next day. Hung arrived wearing a faded raincoat, asked us to switch off the main breaker, and spent five quiet minutes listening and checking the wiring with a tiny pocket multimeter. Rather than guessing, he ruled out the motor coil first and spotted a swollen starter capacitor within ten minutes. Since no spare parts shop was open, he fetched a matching capacitor from an unused old fan in his shed, checked the voltage rating carefully, soldered the joints cleanly, and sealed them with waterproof tape. Within half an hour, water was flowing smoothly again. What I respect most about him isn't just technical skill, but his utter calm under pressure. He never wastes energy panicking or blaming bad luck; he observes, isolates the cause, and works with what's on hand. Having someone that grounded in your circle reminds you that most everyday crises are far more manageable than they first appear.

band8Sample.text: A couple of years ago, during a solo weekend trip to Hoi An, I met a Polish urban planner named Tomasz, and spending an afternoon chatting with him turned out to be the highlight of the whole trip. We struck up a conversation over breakfast at a small family-run guesthouse after both of us happened to ask the host about renting bicycles to explore the countryside. Since we were heading along the same riverside lane, we decided to cycle out through the rice paddies together and stopped for iced coffee under a banyan tree halfway through. What made talking to Tomasz so effortless was his genuine curiosity. Rather than making hasty comparisons with Europe, he kept noticing subtle details I normally took for granted—like how narrow Vietnamese tube houses use internal courtyards to pull cool air through the building, or how plastic stools transform a quiet pavement into a lively social hub after dusk. In return, he told me about winter life in Krakow, traditional Christmas Eve carp dinners, and how Polish towns are gradually pedestrianising old market squares to cut car traffic. We must have talked for nearly four hours about architecture, coffee culture, and how rapidly both our countries have changed since our parents' generation. The encounter stayed with me because it punctured a lot of vague textbook ideas I had about cultural differences. Yes, our climates, languages, and cuisines couldn't be further apart, yet our everyday worries—affordable flats, walkable streets, finding time for family—were strikingly similar. Meeting someone that open-minded reminded me why travelling slowly and talking to strangers beats rushing through tourist checklists.

band8Sample.text: I'd like to talk about my close friend Khanh, whom I've known for roughly eight years since we shared a cramped dormitory corridor in our first year at university. We've always got on effortlessly, yet I only realised how steadfast a friend he truly is about three years ago, during one of the roughest patches of my early career. At the time, the small startup I'd poured eighteen months into ran out of funding almost overnight, and I suddenly found myself unemployed while also recovering from a bad bout of burnout. I was feeling deeply embarrassed and started withdrawing from group chats because I didn't want to field well-meaning questions about my next move. Khanh noticed the silence straight away. Instead of bombarding me with cheerful slogans about everything happening for a reason, he simply turned up at my flat on a Tuesday evening with two bowls of hot noodle soup and suggested we go for a slow walk along the canal. Over the next month, he checked in twice a week like clockwork. On some nights he just listened while I vented; on others, he sat beside me at a café, quietly helped me trim my rambling CV down to one sharp page, and ran two mock technical interviews with me so I wouldn't freeze up in the real ones. What mattered most was that he treated my setback as a temporary logistical hurdle rather than a personal failure. Once I landed a new role, our friendship felt noticeably deeper—the kind where you don't need to perform or put on a brave face. That period taught me that real loyalty shows up in quiet, practical consistency.

band8Sample.text: I'd love to describe an independent ceramicist named Trang whose studio sits tucked down a leafy lane on the outskirts of my city. I first stumbled across her work two years ago at a small weekend design fair, where her display table stood out immediately from the glossy factory-made pottery nearby. Her teacups and bowls were matte, earthy, and slightly irregular around the rim, glazed in muted shades of moss green and warm river clay. I ended up buying a pair of espresso cups and chatting with her for twenty minutes, and later I even joined one of her Saturday morning workshops to see how she works. What makes Trang's approach so distinctive is her obsession with local materials and natural imperfection. Instead of importing bright chemical pigments, she experiments with wood ash, crushed granite dust, and rice-husk glaze, keeping meticulous notebooks of kiln temperatures and firing times. She told us that roughly one in five pieces still cracks or warps in the kiln, yet she treats those failures as data rather than disasters. Watching her centre wet clay on the wheel with calm, unhurried precision was almost hypnotic—there's nowhere to hide a rushed gesture when you're working by hand. I admire her dedication enormously because making a living from slow, small-batch craftsmanship in an era of cheap overnight delivery takes real courage. Every morning when I hold one of her sturdy little cups, I'm reminded of the human patience baked into it, and it has honestly made me far more selective about the objects I bring into my home.

band8Sample.text: My favourite quiet refuge in the city is the third-floor reading room of our municipal public library, tucked just behind a busy central boulevard. From the outside, you'd expect the noise of motorbikes and buses to pour straight in, yet the moment you climb the wide terrazzo staircase and push open the heavy timber doors, the city seems to drop to a whisper. The room itself has wonderfully high ceilings, tall arched windows looking out into the leafy canopy of old tamarind trees, and long oak tables fitted with warm brass reading lamps. Unlike trendy cafés, there's no loud pop playlist, no hiss of espresso machines, and no silent pressure to order another pricey drink just to justify sitting there for three hours. I usually head over on Saturday mornings right after it opens at eight, claim a corner seat by the south window, and work through IELTS reading passages or write notes in a paper journal. What keeps the atmosphere so serene is partly the thick colonial-era masonry that absorbs street rumble, and partly an unspoken pact among everyone inside—you'll see retirees flicking gently through newspapers beside university students sketching architectural plans, all respecting the stillness. Spending a morning there acts like a reset button for my brain. Living in a fast-paced metropolis, it's rare to find an indoor space that asks nothing of you financially and lets your thoughts breathe at their own pace. I always walk back down the front steps feeling noticeably clearer-headed and far less rushed than when I arrived.

band8Sample.text: A historic place that made an unforgettable impression on me is Phuoc Tich, an ancient riverside pottery village about forty kilometres north of Hue in central Vietnam. I visited it on a misty weekday morning last spring after a local friend urged me to skip the busier tourist spots and cycle out along the O Lau River instead. Stepping onto its narrow brick lanes felt like entering a quieter century. Unlike heavily commercialised old towns packed with souvenir stalls and neon signs, Phuoc Tich consists of dozens of traditional timber garden houses framed by clipped tea-plant hedges, mossy tiled roofs, and centuries-old banyan trees. Because the village is tucked into a bend of the river, it's remarkably serene—almost the only sounds were birdsong, bicycles rattling softly over brickwork, and the distant splash of oars. While I was there, an elderly homeowner kindly invited me onto his veranda for a cup of bitter lotus tea and showed me the carved wooden beams his great-grandfather had assembled without a single iron nail. Later I wandered past the remnants of traditional wood-fired ceramic kilns that once supplied royal kitchens. What stayed with me most was the feeling of living heritage rather than a staged film set. People still cook, garden, and care for ancestral shrines inside those timber homes, yet you can also sense how fragile that continuity is as younger villagers move to cities for work. Leaving at dusk, I felt a mixture of deep admiration and quiet urgency—the place showed me how much grace traditional vernacular architecture carries when a community manages to preserve its rhythm.

band8Sample.text: One modern structure that completely surprised me is a bamboo community pavilion built beside a quiet canal on the edge of Da Nang, which serves as a venue for lectures, weekend craft fairs, and small acoustic concerts. From across the water, it looks almost like an upturned woven basket or a giant tropical leaf hovering above a shallow reflecting pool. What makes the design so remarkable is that the entire soaring vaulted roof is constructed from thousands of treated bamboo poles lashed and pinned together, with virtually no visible steel girders or concrete columns interrupting the central floor. I first visited on a sweltering afternoon in July for a local photography talk, expecting to roast under a roof without air conditioning. Yet the instant I stepped inside, the temperature felt five or six degrees cooler. Because the pavilion sits over water and features a wide circular oculus at the very top, warm air rises naturally and pulls a gentle breeze across the pool and through the seating area. Soft shafts of daylight filter through the curved lattice, casting shifting geometric patterns across the stone tiles as the sun moves. To my mind, it's a genuinely triumphant piece of architecture because its beauty serves a real environmental and social purpose rather than merely showing off for photographs. Too many futuristic glass towers ignore the tropical sun and rely on roaring cooling plants; this pavilion works with local climate and modest local materials to create a welcoming public hall that feels both rooted and strikingly contemporary.

band8Sample.text: A natural spot I return to whenever I need to clear my head is the Son Tra peninsula, a forested headland jutting into the sea just twenty-five minutes by scooter from central Da Nang. The transition is astonishingly abrupt: one minute you're weaving past coastal cafés, and ten minutes later you're climbing a winding hillside road beneath dense tropical canopy with sheer views down to turquoise rocky coves. Because much of the peninsula is a protected nature reserve, the air smells sharply of damp leaves, wild figs, and sea salt rather than exhaust fumes. If you head up around six in the morning and switch off your engine near the quieter turnouts, you often catch sight of rare red-shanked douc langurs—strikingly colourful monkeys leaping silently between high branches—alongside bright kingfishers darting over forest streams. My favourite routine is riding up with a friend at sunrise, parking near an old banyan trail, and hiking for an hour before sitting on a sun-warmed boulder to share a thermos of hot tea and banh mi while watching fishing boats fan out across the bay below. What makes Son Tra so dear to me is that it offers genuine wilderness right on an urban doorstep, yet it also feels wonderfully fragile. Seeing wild primates thriving just kilometres from high-rise hotels gives me a deep sense of gratitude and a much stronger personal stake in conservation. Every visit resets my sense of scale—work deadlines that felt monumental on Friday evening shrink back to their proper size when you're staring across an endless horizon of sea and cloud.
